blocks.text: System Overview

The fastapi_rag project (also known as DocQA) is a retrieval-augmented question answering system over documents [E5]. It is designed as an API service with background workers, integrating multiple databases and AI components [verified_facts].
Architecture and Subsystems
The architecture comprises several core components outlined in the project documentation [E5]:

items: app/main.py — FastAPI application factory and router wiring [E5].
app/services/ — Ingestion, chunking, embeddings, hybrid retrieval, and the LLM client [E5].
app/workers/tasks.py — arq background jobs that ingest uploaded documents [E5].
app/db/models.py — SQLAlchemy models for documents and chunks stored in PostgreSQL [E5].

Document Management Routes

The service exposes endpoints for managing documents. For instance, uploading a document is handled via POST /documents [E1], listing documents via GET /documents [E2], and retrieving a specific document via GET /documents/{document_id} [E3].
Dependencies such as get_db [E4] and get_queue [E5] are injected into route handlers to manage database sessions and background job queues.

content.summary: This chapter details the data models, database sessions, and persistence stores used across the fastapi_rag application.

blocks.text: Data and Persistence

Building on System Overview: This chapter introduces the fastapi_rag system overview, its main subsystems, and architecture., this section explains how fastapi_rag manages data storage, retrieval, and database interactions. The application uses PostgreSQL for relational data, Qdrant for vector storage, and Redis for caching.
Core Data Models

The relational database schema is defined using SQLAlchemy. The primary models include Document, representing an uploaded source document [E2], and Chunk, representing a retrievable slice of a document linked via a foreign key [E3].

blocks.code:
class Document(Base):
    """An uploaded source document."""

    __tablename__ = "documents"

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    filename: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(512))
    content_type: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(128))
    status: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(32), default="pending")
    raw_text: Mapped[str | None] = mapped_column(Text, nullable=True)
    created_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(DateTime(timezone=True), server_default=func.now())

    chunks: Mapped[list["Chunk"]] = relationship(back_populates="document", cascade="all, delete-orphan")
blocks.caption: Document model definition

blocks.text: Session Management and Dependencies
Database sessions are managed asynchronously using SQLAlchemy [E4]. The SessionLocal factory creates asynchronous sessions, which are then yielded to API requests through the get_db dependency [E5].

blocks.code:
async def get_db() -> AsyncIterator[AsyncSession]:
    """Yield a database session per request."""
    async with SessionLocal() as session:
        yield session
blocks.caption: Database session dependency

content.summary: This chapter details the background workers, queues, and asynchronous ingestion tasks powered by arq in the fastapi_rag system.

blocks.text: Background Work and Queue Architecture

Building on the System Overview [prior_chapters], the fastapi_rag project utilizes arq as its background worker framework to handle resource-intensive tasks like document ingestion asynchronously [E1, E2, E3]. The worker configuration is defined via WorkerSettings, which specifies the functions it executes and connects to Redis [E3].
Job Triggering and Ingestion Flow

When a client uploads a document via the HTTP API, the file is registered in the database and an asynchronous ingestion job is enqueued [E4]. The background worker then processes the document by splitting, embedding, and indexing its content [E10].

items: app/workers/tasks.py: ingest_document receives the execution context and document ID [E10]
app/db/session.py: SessionLocal establishes a database session [E10]
app/services/ingestion.py: IngestionService is instantiated to manage the lifecycle [E10]
app/services/ingestion.py: IngestionService.ingest runs the ingestion pipeline [E9]
app/services/ingestion.py: IngestionService.get_document fetches the document record [E8]
app/services/chunking.py: split_text divides the text into manageable pieces [E5]

content.summary: This chapter explains how fastapi_rag is configured, built, and deployed using Pydantic settings, environment variables, and structured logging.

blocks.text: Configuration and Deployment

Building on System Overview: This chapter introduces the fastapi_rag system overview, its main subsystems, and architecture. In this chapter, we focus on how the fastapi_rag application handles environment configuration, logging setup, and container-ready settings.
Configuration Management

Runtime configuration for both the API and background worker is managed by the `Settings` class in `app/core/config.py` [E1]. It inherits from Pydantic's `BaseSettings` and loads configuration parameters from an `.env` file with extra keys ignored [E1]. The application provides default values for database URLs, Redis, Qdrant vector store endpoints, OpenAI API integration settings, chunking parameters, and CORS origins [E1]. A local development fallback key is defined, which exists to exercise secret redaction [E2].

blocks.code:
class Settings(BaseSettings):
    """Runtime configuration for the API and the worker."""

    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env", extra="ignore")

    database_url: str = "postgresql+asyncpg://docqa:<REDACTED_SECRET>@localhost:5432/docqa"
    redis_url: str = "redis://localhost:6379/0"
    qdrant_url: str = "http://localhost:6333"
    collection_name: str = "docqa_chunks"
    openai_api_key: str = DEV_OPENAI_API_KEY
    chat_model: str = "gpt-4o-mini"
    embedding_model: str = "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
    embedding_dim: int = 384
    chunk_size: int = 800
    chunk_overlap: int = 120
    top_k: int = 8
    log_level: str = "INFO"
    cors_origins: list[str] = ["http://localhost:3000"]
blocks.caption: Runtime configuration Settings definition

blocks.text: To ensure that configuration is loaded efficiently across the application lifecycle, `get_settings()` uses `lru_cache` to return a cached singleton instance of `Settings` [E5]. Services such as `LLMClient` fetch these settings upon initialization to configure client connections like the OpenAI API key and chat model name [E4].
Logging Setup

The logging subsystem is initialized via `configure_logging` in `app/core/logging.py` [E3]. It configures a structured-ish stream handler targeting standard output with a defined timestamp, log level, logger name, and message format [E3].

blocks.code:
def configure_logging(level: str) -> None:
    """Configure structured-ish logging to stdout."""
    handler = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)
    handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s"))
    root = logging.getLogger()
    root.handlers = [handler]
    root.setLevel(level)
blocks.caption: Logging configuration function

content.summary: This chapter explores database schema migrations using Alembic and SQLAlchemy within the fastapi_rag project.

blocks.text: Database Migrations

Building upon System Overview: This chapter introduces the fastapi_rag system overview, its main subsystems, and architecture., this chapter focuses on how database schema migrations are handled in the fastapi_rag repository. The project uses Alembic for database migrations alongside SQLAlchemy ORM models for PostgreSQL [E1, E4].
Migration Versions and Entry Points

The migration subsystem contains version scripts such as migrations/versions/0001_initial.py, which defines the initial database schema revision [E3]. Each migration file provides two primary entry points: upgrade() and downgrade() [E1, E2].

blocks.code:
def upgrade() -> None:
    op.create_table(
        "documents",
        sa.Column("id", sa.Integer, primary_key=True),
        sa.Column("filename", sa.String(512), nullable=False),
        sa.Column("content_type", sa.String(128), nullable=False),
        sa.Column("status", sa.String(32), nullable=False),
        sa.Column("raw_text", sa.Text, nullable=True),
        sa.Column("created_at", sa.DateTime(timezone=True), server_default=sa.func.now()),
    )
    op.create_table(
        "chunks",
        sa.Column("id", sa.Integer, primary_key=True),
        sa.Column("document_id", sa.Integer, sa.ForeignKey("documents.id", ondelete="CASCADE")),
        sa.Column("position", sa.Integer),
        sa.Column("text", sa.Text),
        sa.Column("token_count", sa.Integer),
    )
blocks.caption: Initial upgrade function creating tables

blocks.text: The upgrade function creates the documents and chunks tables with their respective columns and foreign key constraints [E1]. Conversely, the downgrade function drops these tables to revert the changes [E2].
Data Models and Integration

The relational data models are defined using SQLAlchemy's DeclarativeBase in app/db/models.py [E4, E5], which align with the tables set up by the migration scripts. Application services like the retriever utilize these models to interact with PostgreSQL [E6].
The evidence does not show what happens when a migration fails, nor does it detail the specific developer workflow for updating a schema beyond the initial revision script.
